sources.rank_basis: tier B, rated from the saved page. It is the nftables project's own wiki on the project's domain ('From nftables wiki'), so rank 1 (a project's own docs site) fits. But it is a MediaWiki page with no author, maintainer or review shown (Log in, Discussion, View history), so rank 3 (curated reference, like MDN) also fits. Two ranks fit, so the higher number, 3, is taken. Rank 6 was rejected: this is project-hosted documentation, not a forum, Q&A or personal post, and anonymous editing is off ('View source').
A local lab artifact (a repo path, no URL), missing from stage1.json and with no saved text. Claims citing only it are not_checkable.

claim_checks.claim: Artifact: interface and socket views (lab, Linux 6.17.8, 2026-11-04)
claim_checks.page_says: not checkable: cites only the local lab artifact [^6]

claim_checks.claim: NIC (network interface card) — its job: receive frames and write them into RAM, via DMA into receive ring buffers; with RSS, it hashes flows over several queues, each with its own interrupt
claim_checks.page_says: Each receive queue has a separate IRQ associated with it. | The filter used in RSS is typically a hash function over the network and/or transport layer headers
claim_checks.note: The per-queue IRQ and RSS hashing are supported, though the page says the filter is 'typically' a hash. 'Write them into RAM, via DMA' is not found: searched 'DMA', 'RAM' and 'memory' in [^2]. No cached page mentions DMA.

claim_checks.claim: Driver + NAPI — its job: turn interrupts into batched polling, via napi_schedule() and a poll function with a packet budget
claim_checks.page_says: In basic operation the device notifies the host about new events via an interrupt. The host then schedules a NAPI instance to process the events.
claim_checks.note: The page also says napi_schedule() 'is the basic method of scheduling a NAPI poll' and that the poll method 'takes a budget argument'.

claim_checks.claim: Protocol stack (IP, TCP/UDP) — its job: validate, route, filter and demultiplex packets to sockets, via the kernel's per-packet buffer structure (sk_buff)
claim_checks.page_says: sk_buff is the main networking structure representing a packet.
claim_checks.note: Only the sk_buff part is supported. The stack's job (validate, route, filter, demultiplex to sockets) is not found in [^7]: searched 'validat', 'demultiplex', 'socket', 'rout'.

claim_checks.claim: Netfilter — its job: let firewall/NAT rules inspect packets at fixed hooks, via prerouting, input, forward, output and postrouting
claim_checks.page_says: Traffic flowing to the local machine in the input path sees the prerouting and input hooks. | Such forwarded packets follow the path: prerouting, forward and postrouting.
claim_checks.note: The page also names the output and postrouting path for locally generated traffic, and the NAT engine and filter/nat chain types at these hooks. It adds ingress and egress hooks, but the claim does not say the five are the only ones.

claim_checks.claim: Socket — its job: buffer data between the stack and the application, via receive and send buffers sized by tcp_rmem / tcp_wmem
claim_checks.page_says: initial size of receive buffer used by TCP sockets. This value overrides net.core.rmem_default used by other protocols.
claim_checks.note: Wider scope: tcp_rmem and tcp_wmem size TCP sockets only, and other protocols use net.core.rmem_default and wmem_default. The claim drops the 'TCP' qualifier.

claim_checks.claim: With RSS, the NIC hashes header fields to pick one of several receive queues, so different flows land on different CPUs
claim_checks.page_says: The filter used in RSS is typically a hash function over the network and/or transport layer headers | which in turn can be processed by separate CPUs
claim_checks.note: Drops 'typically'. The page's 'can be processed by separate CPUs' is written as a plain 'land on different CPUs'. The preceding sentence ('writes frames into a receive ring and raises an interrupt') carries no mark and was not graded.

claim_checks.claim: Driver (interrupt → softirq): the interrupt handler calls napi_schedule() and leaves the device interrupt masked until polling finishes
claim_checks.page_says: Drivers should keep the interrupts masked after scheduling the NAPI instance - until NAPI polling finishes any further interrupts are unnecessary.
claim_checks.note: Both parts are SHOULD rules on the page ('Drivers should call this function in their interrupt handler'; 'should keep the interrupts masked'). The claim states them as plain behaviour.

claim_checks.claim: NAPI poll (softirq): processes up to a budget of packets per call; if work remains it is polled again, otherwise napi_complete_done() re-enables interrupts
claim_checks.page_says: napi_complete_done() releases the ownership of the instance. | IRQ should only be unmasked after a successful call to napi_complete_done(): | arm a repoll timer instead of unmasking the hardware interrupts
claim_checks.note: The page gives napi_complete_done() a different job: it releases ownership. The driver unmasks the IRQ, and only after a successful call. With IRQ deferral, NAPI arms a repoll timer instead of unmasking. The budget part also overstates: the page limits only Rx packets ('should only process up to budget number of Rx packets'), and Tx completions are unlimited.

claim_checks.claim: Polling normally runs in softirq context; threaded NAPI moves it to kernel threads
claim_checks.page_says: NAPI processing usually happens in the software interrupt context, but there is an option to use separate kernel threads for NAPI processing.

claim_checks.claim: If the hardware has one queue, RPS can spread protocol processing to other CPUs in software
claim_checks.page_says: RPS selects the CPU to perform protocol processing above the interrupt handler. | For a single queue device, a typical RPS configuration would be to set the rps_cpus
claim_checks.note: The page also calls RPS 'logically a software implementation of RSS'.

claim_checks.claim: IP layer: packets pass netfilter's prerouting hook, then a routing decision sends them to input (for this host) or forward (to another interface)
claim_checks.page_says: do not forget to enable forwarding | Then packets that are not addressed to your local system will be seen from the forward hook.
claim_checks.note: Dropped condition: the page reaches the forward hook only after forwarding is enabled (ip_forward). The claim states the split with no condition.

claim_checks.claim: nat PREROUTING alters packets "as soon as they come in", before routing
claim_checks.page_says: This table is consulted when a packet that creates a new connection is encountered. It consists of four built-ins: PREROUTING (for altering packets as soon as they come in)
claim_checks.note: Dropped qualifier: the nat table is consulted only for a packet that creates a new connection. 'Before routing' is supported by the mangle PREROUTING entry ('altering incoming packets before routing').

claim_checks.claim: The default TCP receive buffer is 128 KiB (tcp_rmem middle value 131072), growing up to a memory-dependent maximum
claim_checks.page_says: initial size of receive buffer used by TCP sockets. This value overrides net.core.rmem_default used by other protocols. Default: 131072 bytes. | Default: between 131072 and 32MB, depending on RAM size.
claim_checks.note: Auto-tuning up to tcp_rmem[2] is on by default (tcp_moderate_rcvbuf 'Default: 1 (enabled)'). The preceding sentence (TCP/UDP finds the socket by address and port) carries no mark and was not graded.

claim_checks.claim: Application: recv() copies data out of the buffer. If the application reads too slowly, the buffer fills and TCP advertises a smaller window, slowing the sender
claim_checks.page_says: not checkable: cites only the local lab artifact [^6]

claim_checks.claim: Transmit: send() copies into the send buffer (default 16 KiB in tcp_wmem)
claim_checks.page_says: initial size of send buffer used by TCP sockets. | Default: 16K | sendmsg() will also not add new buffers if the limit is hit.

claim_checks.claim: TCP segments the data, IP routes it, it passes the output and postrouting hooks
claim_checks.page_says: the traffic that is generated by local processes follows the output and postrouting path.
claim_checks.note: The hooks are supported. TCP segmentation and IP routing are not found in [^3]: searched 'segment', 'rout'. The order 'IP routes it, it passes the output ... hooks' also clashes with [^8] (OUTPUT is 'for altering locally-generated packets before routing') and with the doc's own diagram (output ─► ROUTING).

claim_checks.claim: XPS picks the transmit queue from the sending CPU
claim_checks.page_says: Alternatively, this function can also use the ID of the running CPU as a key into the CPU-to-queue lookup table. | XPS is only available if the kconfig symbol CONFIG_XPS is enabled
claim_checks.note: Dropped conditions: XPS first tries the socket's receive-queue map, uses the CPU map only 'alternatively', needs CONFIG_XPS and driver or admin setup, and 'has no effect' on a single-queue device. The preceding clause (qdisc and driver put it on the transmit ring) carries no mark, and no cached page backs it.

claim_checks.claim: A two-namespace setup in the lab shows a packet's path from a "container" to the internet (Linux 6.17.8, 2026-11-04)
claim_checks.page_says: not checkable: cites only the local lab artifact [^6]

claim_checks.claim: veth pair: a frame sent into veth-c appears on its peer veth-h in the host namespace
claim_checks.page_says: Packets transmitted on one device in the pair are immediately received on the other device.
claim_checks.note: The page also describes placing the two ends in different namespaces.

claim_checks.claim: Host routing: destination is not local → forward (needs ip_forward = 1, default 0)
claim_checks.page_says: Forward Packets between interfaces. | Default: 0 (disabled)
claim_checks.note: The ip_forward part is supported. The routing rule 'destination is not local → forward' is not in [^4]. It is in [^3] ('packets that are not addressed to your local system will be seen from the forward hook'), which this step does not cite.

claim_checks.claim: One CPU at 100% in si (softirq) while others idle | Throughput capped by one core | All flows on one RX queue; spread with RSS/RPS
claim_checks.page_says: RSS should be enabled when latency is a concern or whenever receive interrupt processing forms a bottleneck. | in which case packets are processed on the interrupting CPU
claim_checks.note: The remedy and the single-CPU processing are supported. The 'si' symptom and the throughput cap are not stated: searched 'softirq', 'si'.

claim_checks.claim: RX ring overflows | Counted as missed/dropped on the interface (ip -s link) | Buffer exhaustion is counted in rx_missed_errors
claim_checks.page_says: should not include packets dropped by the device due to buffer exhaustion which are counted separately in rx_missed_errors | next buffer in the ring was not available for a scatter transfer
claim_checks.note: The rx_missed_errors part is supported. But the page also maps ring-buffer unavailability to rx_over_errors (shown as 'overrun' by ip -s link), so 'counted as missed/dropped' leaves out a counter.

claim_checks.claim: Recv-Q growing on an established socket | Application is not reading | Data waits in the socket buffer
claim_checks.page_says: not checkable: cites only the local lab artifact [^6]

claim_checks.claim: Forwarding between namespaces does not work | Packets dropped at routing | ip_forward is 0 by default
claim_checks.page_says: Forward Packets between interfaces. | Default: 0 (disabled)
claim_checks.note: The default of 0 is supported. 'Packets dropped at routing' is not found in [^4]: searched 'drop', 'forward'.

claim_checks.claim: Busy polling enabled | Lower latency, more CPU | Apps poll before the interrupt fires
claim_checks.page_says: Busy polling allows a user process to check for incoming packets before the device interrupt fires. | it trades off CPU cycles for lower latency

claim_checks.claim: "Connection refused" vs timeout | Refused = an RST came back (no listener); timeout = packets dropped silently (firewall, routing) | Lab: closed port → "Connection refused" at once; port behind an iptables DROP → "timed out" after 3 s
claim_checks.page_says: not checkable: cites only the local lab artifact [^6]

claim_checks.claim: RSS/RPS across all CPUs | Parallel packet processing | Cache misses if the app runs on another CPU (RFS mitigates)
claim_checks.page_says: The goal of RFS is to increase datacache hitrate by steering kernel processing of packets to the CPU where the application thread consuming the packet is running.
claim_checks.note: The page also says RPS 'does not take into account application locality'.

claim_checks.claim: Busy polling / threaded NAPI pinned | Lower, steadier latency | Burns a core
claim_checks.page_says: it trades off CPU cycles for lower latency | Note that this will keep the CPU core busy with 100% usage.
claim_checks.note: 'Steadier' is not found. The 100% core applies to a threaded busy-polling kthread pinned to an unused core. For plain pinned threaded NAPI, the page claims neither a latency gain nor a burned core.

violations.evidence: C2: 'write them into RAM, via DMA' is not in [^2]. No cached page mentions DMA.
C4: [^7] supports only 'sk_buff is the main networking structure representing a packet', not the stack's validate/route/filter/demultiplex job.

C9: [^1] says napi_complete_done() 'releases the ownership of the instance'. The driver unmasks the IRQ only after a successful call, or NAPI arms a repoll timer instead. The claim says napi_complete_done() re-enables interrupts.
C17: 'TCP segments the data, IP routes it' is not in [^3]. The order (routing before the output hook) also clashes with [^8] and with the doc's diagram.
C21: the rule 'destination is not local → forward' is not in [^4]. It is supported by [^3], which this step does not cite.
C6: tcp_rmem/tcp_wmem size TCP sockets only. The claim applies them to sockets in general.
C7: drops 'typically' from the RSS hash and turns 'can be processed by separate CPUs' into a plain statement.
C8: the page's SHOULD rules (call napi_schedule() in the IRQ handler; keep interrupts masked) are written as plain behaviour.
C12: drops the condition that forwarding must be enabled before packets reach the forward hook.
C13: drops the qualifier that the nat table is consulted only for a packet that creates a new connection.
C18: XPS uses the CPU map only 'alternatively' to the receive-queue map, needs CONFIG_XPS and setup, and has no effect on a single-queue device. The claim states it unconditionally.
C22: the si symptom and the throughput cap are not stated in [^2].
C23: [^9] also maps ring-buffer unavailability to rx_over_errors ('overrun'), which the row leaves out.
C25: 'Packets dropped at routing' is not in [^4].
C29: 'steadier' is not in [^1], and the burned-core cost belongs to threaded busy polling, not to plain pinned threaded NAPI.

No role 5 (reference and invariants) section: exact values (tcp_rmem, tcp_wmem, ip_forward, drop counters) are scattered through the steps. Role 2 content (the 6-actor list) is merged into the mechanism section.
